description_top: Everyone has drawn the URL shortener: a hash, a table, a cache. It is still asked at every level, because the grade is on what comes after the diagram. This is a full reference solution at the Staff bar (L6/L7): theory, a three-version design, eight challenges that break it, and the build cost. {DURATION} minutes, {SLIDES} numbered slides, with an interviewer, a candidate and a coach.

The thesis: a URL shortener is a read path with a write path attached. Codes must be unique without a lock per create and unguessable without a lookup, the redirect must be one memory read, and nothing else (counting, abuse, analytics) may stand between the click and the answer.

IN THIS VIDEO
• Estimates as arithmetic: why seven characters (3.5 trillion codes for 12 billion links), 4,000 redirects a second but 40 at the store, 7 of 20 milliseconds
• Theory: safety and liveness, six mechanisms, an options matrix for code generation with a pick (and an honest equal)
• Eight challenges: two servers and one code, codes that can be walked, one link at 40,000 clicks a second, 301 or 302, a takedown everywhere in five minutes, counting without slowing the redirect, a region lost, and how you would know
• The build cost and team split (marked AUX, the manager layer)

HOW TO USE IT
Run the round cold first. Then watch once straight through. On the second pass, pause after each interviewer question and answer it first. Slides badged AUX are the manager layer: skip them in a Staff round.

This is a scripted walkthrough, not a recording of a real interview, and the interviewer, candidate and coach are not real people. The voices are synthetic (Kokoro-82M, generated locally). Script, diagrams and the written design were produced with Claude Code. Numbers are back-of-the-envelope estimates for the exercise, labelled as given, derived, illustrative or initial targets, not any company's real figures, and this is not any company's actual design. The technical content has not been reviewed by a person.

post: Everyone has drawn the URL shortener. The grade is on what happens after the diagram.

I've published a {DURATION}-minute reference solution for the URL shortener question, at the Staff bar: theory, a three-version design, eight challenges, and the build cost, on {SLIDES} numbered slides.
The idea that unlocks it: the redirect is the product. It is one memory read, and counting, takedowns and the edge all live beside it, each with a number on how late it may be.

What it goes into:
→ Why base-62 of a counter is still a counter, and a keyed shuffle that keeps codes unique
→ One link at 40,000 clicks a second: a hot key, not a load problem
→ 301 or 302 as a product decision
→ A phishing link dead everywhere in five minutes, as a sum of cache lifetimes
Best on a second pass: pause after each question and answer it first.
